title: Where your treasure is
hook: where your treasure is, there will your heart be also (Matthew 6:19–21)
tomorrow: can you judge anyone at all? two readings of 'judge not'.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the left hand doesn't know, and gold through a window at night. Today the sermon follows the gold, and asks where it's taking you.
screen: `THE LEFT HAND DOESN'T KNOW.` → `FOLLOW THE GOLD.`

segments.voice: Someone chips in for a friend's fundraiser and starts checking the total twice a day. Someone buys a ticket to a game and suddenly cares about the score. Odd, but it often runs this way: the money goes first, and the caring follows. That's the strange detail in today's line, and yesterday's question. Jesus doesn't say your treasure will follow your heart. He says it the other way around.
screen: `THE MONEY GOES FIRST.` → `THE CARING FOLLOWS.` → `THE OTHER WAY AROUND.`

segments.voice: Here it is in the Sermon on the Mount. "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven." And then: "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." Moth and rust: treasure that rots in a closet or a box. But the puzzle is the last line. The heart doesn't lead. It follows. Put your treasure somewhere, and your heart goes after it. Matthew tells a story that shows it. A rich young man comes to Jesus and asks what good thing he must do to have eternal life. He has kept the commandments. Jesus answers, "go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven." Treasure in heaven, the sermon's own words. And the young man can't. Matthew says "he went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions." His heart was exactly where his treasure was. So, on this reading, the puzzle has its answer: you can't always choose a feeling, but you can choose where the treasure goes. That's the teaching Christians take from it: giving isn't only charity; it's how a heart gets turned. Where the money and time go, the heart is trained to follow. It's one reason giving is treated as a spiritual practice in churches, not just a bill.
screen: `MOTH AND RUST.` · `THE HEART FOLLOWS.` · `THE RICH YOUNG MAN, SORROWFUL.` · `GIVING TURNS THE HEART.` · then, large: `WHERE MY HEART IS.`

segments.voice: Look at one thing near you that you paid for or worked hard for: your phone, a ring, a shelf of books. Ask it quietly where your heart has been going with it. Let the answer come without arguing with it.
Where your treasure is: the place your heart ends up, because in the sermon the heart follows the treasure.
Pocket this: where my heart is, there my treasure has already gone. Five days into the sermon now.
